intro: The newsroom turns economic, tax, legal and local business news into content an owner can use, fast, without giving up accuracy. Researched briefings are ready to review, and the live wire brings in what primary sources published today. Every piece names its sources, states the status of anything not yet law, and goes through the firm's review process.
disclosure: General information only, not tax, legal or investment advice. Rules and figures change, and how they apply depends on your situation, so talk to your own tax and legal advisors before acting. Figures as of November 12, 2026.

sourcePolicy.heading: Where the facts come from
sourcePolicy.summary: Credible and unbiased is a sourcing discipline, not a feeling. The newsroom ranks every source by how close it sits to the thing itself, and the content says which kind it is.
principles: Primary first. The agency, the statute, the final rule, the company's own announcement, the program's own site. Coverage of a thing is a lead to the thing, not a substitute for it.
Two sources for any number that does not come from the primary. If they disagree, say so and use the primary.
Status is a fact. Proposed, introduced, passed one chamber, signed, final rule and effective date are different claims. Most bad financial content comes from blurring them.
Describe effects, not merits. Say what a law does to an owner's plan. Leave whether it is good policy to the owner.
When something is contested, show the official account and the main criticism, both sourced, or leave it out.
Vendor and marketing summaries are pointers only. They are often right and never the citation.

tiers.name: Primary
tiers.use: Cite directly. The agency, the law, the rule, the company or program itself.
tiers.examples: IRS, Treasury, Federal Reserve, Federal Register, Congress.gov, Louisiana Legislature, Louisiana Department of Revenue, a company's own newsroom, a state program's own site

tiers.name: Statistical agency
tiers.use: Cite directly for data. Nonpartisan by charter.
tiers.examples: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Bureau of Economic Analysis, Census Bureau, Congressional Budget Office

tiers.name: Research
tiers.use: Cite for findings, with the setting and the year. Note whether it is peer reviewed or a working paper.
tiers.examples: NBER working papers, peer-reviewed journals, university research centers

tiers.name: Public-interest newsroom
tiers.use: Cite for reporting on state and local events. Check the primary when it exists.

tiers.name: Wire and business press
tiers.use: Cite for event facts and dates. Cross check numbers.

tiers.name: Professional summary
tiers.use: Use to understand a law. Cite the law itself where you can.
tiers.examples: Law firm and CPA firm client alerts, trade associations

tiers.name: Vendor summary
tiers.use: A pointer only. Never the citation.

guardrails.rule: Every number carries its source and the date it was true. If you cannot source it, cut it.
guardrails.why: A wrong number in financial content costs more trust than a missing one.

guardrails.rule: State the legal status of anything that is not settled law: proposed, introduced, passed one chamber, signed, final rule, or effective on a date.
guardrails.why: Treating a bill as law is the most common and most damaging error in this kind of content.

guardrails.rule: No forecasts of interest rates, markets, prices or whether legislation will pass.
guardrails.why: Nobody knows, regulators treat predictions as promissory, and the owners worth having distrust them.

guardrails.rule: No recommendation of any specific investment, product or insurance policy in public content.
guardrails.why: Public content explains what changed and what to ask. Recommendations happen one to one, after the facts of the person are known.

guardrails.rule: Separate the facts from the firm's view, and label the view as a view.
guardrails.why: Readers can tell when opinion is dressed as news, and so can reviewers.

guardrails.rule: Describe what a policy does to an owner's plan, not whether it is good policy. Where a measure is contested, give the official account and the main criticism, both sourced, or leave it out.
guardrails.why: Unbiased is a practice. The firm serves owners of every politics.

guardrails.rule: Never imply that a company, agency or program named in a piece endorses the firm.
guardrails.why: Naming Meta or the IRS for a fact is reporting. Implying a relationship is a problem.

guardrails.rule: Use no client names or client situations, even disguised, without written consent and review.
guardrails.why: A recognizable story is a disclosure.

guardrails.rule: Every piece goes through the firm's review process before it is published. Timeliness comes from pre-cleared frames, not from skipping review.
guardrails.why: The frame is approved once. Only the sourced facts in it change, which is what makes same-week publishing possible.

guardrails.rule: Close with the general-information disclosure, adapted only through the firm's review process.
guardrails.why: Consistency is what makes a disclosure work.

frames.name: Federal Reserve decision
frames.trigger: An FOMC statement or a change in the federal funds target.
frames.hook: Open on the owner's credit line or cash, not on the Fed.
beats: What the Fed did and the date, quoted from its statement.
What that does to the rate on a typical business line of credit and to what idle cash earns, in plain terms.
Where it shows up in a plan: refinancing, the cash reserve, the discount rate inside a buy-sell valuation.
never: Predict the next decision or the direction of markets.
Tell anyone to buy or sell anything.
frames.nextMove: Look up the rate and the reset date on your line of credit this week.

frames.name: Jobs or inflation release
frames.trigger: A BLS or BEA release that moves the conversation.
frames.hook: Open on payroll or pricing inside the owner's company.
beats: The number, the period it covers and the agency, exactly as released.
What it means for wages, hiring or pricing at a company like theirs.
One thing to check in their own numbers.
never: Call a trend from one release.
Say what the Fed will do about it.
frames.nextMove: Compare your last two quarters of payroll and pricing against the release.

frames.name: IRS inflation adjustments
frames.trigger: The IRS announces next year's contribution limits, brackets or exemptions.
frames.hook: Open on what the owner can put away next year.
beats: The new figures and the year they apply to, from the IRS release.
What changes for the owner personally and for the company plan.
The one deadline that follows from it.
never: Round a figure, or state one before the IRS has published it.
frames.nextMove: Update payroll deferrals before the first paycheck of the new year.

frames.name: New law or final rule
frames.trigger: A bill is signed, or a final rule is published in the Federal Register.
frames.hook: Open on the decision the owner now has to make.
beats: What changed, its status and its effective date, from the law or the rule.
Who it affects and who it does not.
What to do now, what can wait, and what is still unknown.
never: Call a bill law before it is signed.
Describe the law as good or bad policy.
frames.nextMove: Bring this to your next meeting with your CPA, with the question written down.

frames.name: Major investment or incentive in the region
frames.trigger: A large project, incentive package or contract award is announced in the region.
frames.hook: Open on the owner whose company could do the work.
beats: What was announced, by whom, where and when, from the announcement itself.
What winning that kind of work takes: bonding, statements, cash, insurance, people.
The risk that grows with the contract: concentration and key person exposure.
never: Imply a relationship with the company named.
frames.nextMove: Ask your CPA and surety agent what it would take to double your bonding line.

frames.name: State mandate or deadline
frames.trigger: A state program sets or changes a requirement for employers.
frames.hook: Open on the owner with employees in that state, wherever the company is based.
beats: The requirement, who it applies to and the deadline, from the program's own site.
The cost of ignoring it, as the program states it.
The alternative the owner may prefer, and why.
never: Quote a penalty from a vendor summary.
Use the deadline as a countdown.
frames.nextMove: Pull last year's headcount by state.

frames.name: A sharp market move
frames.trigger: A large market drop or spike that clients are talking about.
frames.hook: Open on what the plan was built to absorb.
beats: What happened, in one sourced sentence.
Why the plan has a cash reserve and a rebalancing rule, and that both exist for weeks like this.
What not to decide this week.
never: Predict a recovery or a further fall.
Recommend any action on any security.
Publish without review, however fast it feels like it needs to go out.
frames.nextMove: Call me before you change anything, not after.

states.heading: Retirement plan rules by state
states.summary: The money for starting a plan is federal and works the same in every state. What differs by state is the stick: about 15 states require employers without a plan to enroll their workers in a state automatic IRA, with penalties that vary. Louisiana has no mandate.
states.correction: No state was found that offers its own tax credit for starting a 401(k) as of November 2026. The startup, auto-enrollment and employer contribution credits are federal, from SECURE 2.0, and apply in Louisiana exactly as anywhere else. The only state incentive found is Maryland's waiver of its $300 annual report fee for employers that offer a plan. If you hear of a state credit, ask for the statute before repeating it.
states.followTheEmployee: Mandates follow the employee, not the headquarters. A Louisiana company with a remote employee in California or Illinois may be subject to that state's program for that person. Pull headcount by state before assuming you are exempt.

article.title: Louisiana's megaprojects will be won on balance sheets
article.body:
Two of the largest private investments in Louisiana's history are now under way, and both will be built in large part by Louisiana companies that are not Meta or SpaceX.

In Richland Parish, Meta says its data center campus now represents more than $50 billion of investment in the region. The company reports more than $875 million in contracts with Louisiana businesses over the past year, across more than 160 companies, 84% of them in Northeast Louisiana. The work ranges from electrical and paving to utilities. Peak construction is projected at more than 7,500 workers.

In Vermilion Parish, SpaceX announced on August 25 a Starship launch site it calls Starbase Louisiana, about 125,000 acres near Pecan Island. Reported investment is roughly $100 billion. Construction is expected to begin in 2027, with a first launch targeted for 2029. Louisiana Economic Development estimates about 3,000 direct jobs over a decade.

If you own a contracting, trucking, fabrication, electrical, staffing or services company anywhere near either site, you have probably already had this conversation. What gets talked about less is that this kind of work is decided before the bid. It is decided on your balance sheet.

**The work goes to companies that can carry it**

A general contractor on a project this size is not only asking whether you can do the job. They are asking whether you can survive doing it. That question has five parts.

Bonding. Surety underwriters set your bonding capacity largely from your working capital, your net worth and the quality of your financial statements. Owners who take every spare dollar out of the company at year end often find their bonding line is smaller than their ambition. The decision you make about distributions this December is a decision about which contracts you can bid next year.

Statements. A compiled statement may have been enough for the bank. Larger contracts and larger bonds often call for reviewed or audited statements and a work in progress schedule. Moving up a level takes a year of preparation with your CPA, not a week.

Cash. Large projects pay on their schedule, not yours. Payment terms of 45 to 60 days and retainage held until completion are common in subcontracts, so read yours line by line. Payroll, fuel and materials are due every week regardless. Size your credit line to the widest gap between what you have spent and what you have been paid, and know which personal guarantees sit behind it.

Insurance. Subcontract agreements set minimum limits for general liability, auto, workers' compensation and umbrella coverage, and they can be well above what a smaller book of work needed. Price that before you price the bid.

People. One site alone is projected to need more than 7,500 construction workers at its peak. Every company in the region will be hiring from the same pool at the same time, and what you offer beyond the hourly rate starts to decide who stays.

**The risks that do not announce themselves**

The bigger the contract, the more it depends on you personally. If you hold the relationships, sign the indemnity and guarantee the line, then your disability or death in the middle of a contract is not only a family problem. It is a problem for the surety, the general contractor and every employee on the job. A funded buy-sell agreement and key person coverage set at what the company is worth today, not five years ago, are part of being ready for this work.

There is also a valuation trap. One customer that becomes most of your revenue makes the company bigger and can make it worth less to a buyer, because concentration is risk. Decide early how much of the business you are willing to put on one project.

**The tax side moved in your favor**

Two changes help a company gearing up. The federal law signed in July 2025 restored 100% bonus depreciation for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025, with no scheduled phase down, and raised Section 179 expensing to $2.5 million, indexed for inflation. And Louisiana repealed its corporate franchise tax for tax periods beginning on or after January 1, 2026. That tax was measured on capital, so it grew as you kept earnings in the company, the same retained earnings a surety wants to see. Your CPA should run both against the equipment and capital you plan to put to work.

**Where to start this month**

Pull your last two years of statements and ask your CPA and your surety agent one question: what would we need to show to double our bonding line. Their answer is your plan for the next 12 months. Then test the opportunity against Growth, Liquidity and Control before you commit to it.

If you want a second set of eyes on whether your company and your family balance sheet are ready for work this size, send me a note.

briefings.title: The retirement plan math changed. Most owners have not run it.
briefings.status: Draft for the firm's review process
briefings.summary: Federal credits now pay most of the cost of starting a plan, in every state. About 15 states penalize employers with no plan, and the rules follow the employee across state lines. Louisiana has no mandate, and no state credit could be verified. The angle: decide on your own terms while the credits reward choosing to start.

facts.text: Startup credit: for employers with up to 50 employees, 100% of eligible startup and administration costs, up to $5,000 a year for three years. The cap is $250 per eligible non-highly compensated employee, with a floor of $500. Employers with 51 to 100 employees get 50%.
facts.source: IRS, Retirement plans startup costs tax credit

facts.text: Auto-enrollment credit: $500 a year for three years for adding automatic enrollment.
facts.source: IRS, Retirement plans startup costs tax credit

facts.text: Employer contribution credit: up to $1,000 per eligible employee. For employers with up to 50 employees, 100% in years one and two, then 75%, 50% and 25%. No credit for employees with FICA wages over $100,000, as indexed. Reduced for 51 to 100 employees.
facts.source: IRS; PSCA, How do the retirement plan tax credits work

facts.text: The credits are claimed on IRS Form 8881.

2026 limits: 401(k) deferral $24,500, age 50 catch-up $8,000, ages 60 to 63 catch-up $11,250, IRA $7,500. Catch-up contributions must be Roth for employees whose prior year FICA wages exceeded $150,000.
facts.source: Groom Law Group, 2026 retirement plan limits

facts.text: About 15 states require employers without a plan to facilitate a state automatic IRA. Louisiana is not one of them.
facts.source: Multiple 2026 summaries; confirm on each program's site

facts.text: Pew estimated about 760,000 Louisiana private sector workers, roughly 52%, lack a retirement plan at work.

The Automatic IRA Act (H.R. 6722), introduced in the House in December 2025, would require employers with ten or more employees to offer an automatic arrangement, with consequences from 2028. No committee action found.

The startup credit was created in 2001, its cap was raised from $500 to $5,000 by the SECURE Act in 2019, and SECURE 2.0 raised it to 100% of costs for employers with up to 50 employees in 2022. The 2025 tax law left it unchanged.
A study of Danish savers found each dollar of retirement tax subsidy raised total saving by about one cent, while automatic employer contributions raised wealth substantially.
facts.source: Chetty and others, Quarterly Journal of Economics (2014)

facts.text: Maryland waives its $300 annual report fee for employers that offer a plan, the only state incentive found.

verify: The IRS pages could not be opened from the studio's build environment. Read the startup credit page and Form 8881 instructions and confirm each figure before publishing.
The list of mandate states comes from summaries, one of them a vendor's. Confirm any state named in a piece on its program's own site.
The California penalty is consistent across sources but should be confirmed on CalSavers before it is quoted.
H.R. 6722's status should be checked on Congress.gov on the day of publishing. Sources disagree on its sponsor, so the piece does not name one.
Confirm the $500 credit in the Automatic IRA Act against the bill text. Summaries describe it, and none found says the bill repeals the existing credits.
The startup credit comes from SECURE 2.0 (December 2022), building on the SECURE Act (2019). It is not from the 2025 tax law, which left it unchanged. Do not attribute it to the 2025 law.

evidence.question: If a state can penalize an employer for not having a plan, will the federal incentive to start one go away soon.
evidence.verdict: No credible source says it will, and the firm's own rules forbid predicting legislation. The evidence supports a narrower claim, and the article makes only that one: the one federal mandate proposal pairs a requirement with a much smaller credit, economists find defaults work better than subsidies, and the credits are time-limited for each employer regardless. Against the stronger claim: the credits have grown for 25 years alongside state mandates, the 2025 law left them alone, and mandates are pushing employers into the very plans that earn the credit.

supports.point: The only federal mandate proposal pairs a requirement for employers with ten or more employees with a proposed $500 a year credit for three years, against up to $5,000 a year under today's startup credit. Introduced December 15, 2025 and referred to Ways and Means; no further action found.
supports.source: H.R. 6722, Automatic IRA Act of 2025, bill text

supports.point: Same bill, summarized by the plan sponsor trade association.
supports.source: PSCA, Federal auto-IRA legislation introduced in House (December 2025)

supports.point: Each dollar of government spending on retirement tax subsidies raised total saving by about one cent; automatic employer contributions raised wealth substantially. About 85% of people are passive savers who do not respond to subsidies. The standard evidence for favoring defaults over incentives.
supports.source: Chetty, Friedman, Leth-Petersen, Nielsen and Olsen, Quarterly Journal of Economics (2014); NBER Working Paper 18565

supports.point: The credits are limited by design: the startup credit runs for the first three years of a plan, the contribution credit phases down over five, and neither is available if the employer had a qualified plan in the prior three years.
Retirement tax breaks are among the largest tax expenditures and are under scrutiny: a July 2026 bill would limit very large retirement accounts. That bill does not touch the small employer credits.
supports.source: Rep. Neal press release, July 22, 2026; CRFB on JCT tax expenditures

against.point: The credit has only grown: created in 2001, made permanent in 2006, cap raised from $500 to $5,000 in 2019, raised to 100% of costs for employers with up to 50 employees in 2022. Those are the years states were adding mandates.
against.source: RSM, What does SECURE 2.0 mean for small employers

against.point: The 2025 tax law did not change the startup or contribution credits.
against.source: NAPA, Senate's One Big Beautiful Bill spares retirement plans (June 2025); TXCPA, SECURE 2.0 and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (January 2026)

against.point: State mandates increased new private plan formation, mostly at small and mid-sized firms, with no sign of employers shifting to the state option. Mandates are pushing employers into the plans that earn the federal credit, so today the two work together.
against.source: Bloomfield, Goodman, Rao and Slavov, NBER Working Paper 32817 (2024); Georgetown CRI summary

against.point: Joining a state program does not forfeit the federal credit later. A state auto-IRA is not a qualified plan for the three-year lookback.
against.source: NAPA, Case of the week: CalSavers plan and the federal plan startup tax credit (January 2023)

against.point: No 2026 budget, reconciliation or repeal proposal targeting these credits was found.
against.source: Search of 2026 budget and reconciliation coverage, November 12, 2026

context.point: Only 1% to 5.5% of apparently eligible firms claim the startup credit, depending on the period studied.
context.source: Bloomfield, Goodman, Ramnath and Slavov, Georgetown CRI (2025)

evidence.say: The credits that exist today are the most generous Congress has offered. The one federal mandate proposal pairs a requirement with a smaller credit. Nobody can tell you whether that becomes law. What is certain is your own clock: the credits run for three to five years from when you start.
dontSay: This is a credit from the 2025 tax law.

article.title: The retirement plan math changed. Most owners have not run it.
article.body:
If you own a company with employees and no retirement plan, the federal government will now pay most of the cost of starting one. That has been true since the SECURE 2.0 changes took effect in 2023, and it applies in every state, Louisiana included. Most owners I talk to have not run the numbers.

**What the credits pay**

Three federal credits stack.

The startup credit covers 100% of eligible setup and administration costs for employers with up to 50 employees, for three years. The yearly cap is $250 for each eligible employee who is not highly compensated, with a floor of $500 and a ceiling of $5,000. Employers with 51 to 100 employees get 50%.

The auto-enrollment credit adds $500 a year for three years if the plan enrolls employees automatically.

The employer contribution credit pays up to $1,000 per eligible employee toward what you contribute for them. For employers with up to 50 employees it covers the full amount in the first two years, then 75%, 50% and 25% in years three, four and five. Employees with more than $100,000 in FICA wages, as indexed, do not count, which in most cases means it does not cover what you put in for yourself.

All three are claimed on IRS Form 8881, and they generally require that you have not had a plan in the prior three years. Your CPA should confirm eligibility before you count on any of it.

**What states are doing instead**

About 15 states now require employers without a plan to enroll their workers in a state-run automatic IRA, among them California, Illinois, Oregon, Maryland, Virginia, New York and New Jersey. Penalties vary by state. California's law sets $250 per eligible employee once the deadline passes, and $500 more per employee if the employer is still out of compliance 90 days later. Check the program's own site before quoting any figure, because they change.

Louisiana has no mandate. Pew estimated in 2024 that about 760,000 Louisiana private sector workers, roughly 52%, have no retirement plan at work.

Here is the part that catches Louisiana owners. The mandates follow the employee, not the headquarters. If you have a remote employee in California or Illinois, you may already be subject to that state's program for that person.

And for the record: I could not find a state that offers its own tax credit for starting a plan. The closest is Maryland, which waives its $300 annual report fee for employers that offer one. The money is federal.

**The direction of travel**

Owners ask me a fair question here. If states can penalize you for not having a plan, how long will Washington keep paying you to start one.

Nobody knows, and I will not pretend to. What the record shows is worth knowing anyway.

The credits have grown, not shrunk. The startup credit dates to 2001. Congress raised its cap from $500 to $5,000 in 2019 and raised it again to 100% of costs for smaller employers in 2022, in the same years states were adding mandates. The federal tax law signed in July 2025 left these credits alone.

The one federal mandate on the table pairs a requirement with a smaller incentive. The Automatic IRA Act, introduced in the House in December 2025, would require employers with ten or more employees to offer an automatic arrangement, and it proposes a credit of $500 a year for three years for those arrangements. Today's startup credit can be worth up to $5,000 a year. The bill has not advanced, and it may never pass.

The economics favor defaults over subsidies. A widely cited study of Danish savers found that each dollar of tax subsidy raised total saving by about one cent, while automatic employer contributions raised it substantially. That finding is a large part of why policy has moved toward automatic enrollment.

And the credit is time-limited for you, whatever Congress does. The startup credit covers the first three years of a new plan, and the contribution credit phases down over five. The clock starts when you start.

That is not a reason to rush. It is a reason to decide on your own terms, while the credits are built to reward owners who choose to start.

**Why a state IRA is not your answer**

A state automatic IRA is a reasonable floor for employees. It does little for you as the owner. The 2026 IRA limit is $7,500. The 401(k) deferral limit is $24,500, with $8,000 more in catch-up contributions from age 50 and $11,250 for ages 60 through 63. State programs do not allow an employer match, which also takes away one of the better recruiting tools you have. With one construction site in Richland Parish projected to need more than 7,500 workers at its peak, that matters in Louisiana right now.

One more 2026 change. If your prior year FICA wages from the company were over $150,000, your catch-up contributions now have to go in as Roth.

**Your next move**

Pull last year's headcount and sort it two ways: by the state each employee works in, and by who earned under $100,000. Those two lists tell you whether any mandate applies and roughly what the credits are worth. Then decide whether a plan fits your priorities for Growth, Liquidity and Control over the next three years.

If you want me to run the numbers with your CPA, reply to this and we will set up 30 minutes.

article.title: The estate tax number stopped moving. Your plan should not.
article.body:
For most of the last decade, estate planning for business owners had a deadline built into it. The federal exemption was scheduled to fall roughly in half at the start of 2026, and a lot of planning was rushed to beat it.

That deadline is gone. The federal law signed on July 4, 2025 set the estate and gift tax exemption at $15 million per person for 2026, $30 million for a married couple, indexed for inflation from 2027, with no scheduled expiration. Congress can change any law, but for the first time in years there is no sunset on the calendar.

For a lot of owners, that changes the question from how fast to how well.

**What did not change**

Your company is still most of what you own, and its value is still the number everything else depends on. If your buy-sell agreement was set at a figure from years ago, it decides who gets what at a price nobody agreed to today. And if most of your wealth is in the business, your family still needs cash it can reach: for taxes above the exemption, for buying out a sibling who does not want the company, or for running it through a hard year without you.

**Where the new rules open room**

The larger exemption gives you room to move ownership to the next generation, or into trusts, while the company's value is still growing, without an immediate tax bill.

The same law also expanded the exclusion for qualified small business stock issued after July 4, 2025. The cap rose to $15 million, companies with up to $75 million in assets can qualify, and a partial exclusion now begins after three years instead of five. If you are forming a new entity or raising capital, the structure you choose now can matter a great deal at exit. That is a conversation for your attorney and CPA together, before the paperwork, not after.

**State lines still matter**

Louisiana has no estate tax and no inheritance tax. Several other states do, often with exemptions far below the federal number. If you own property elsewhere or plan to retire somewhere else, that state's rules can matter more than the federal ones.

**Your next move**

Find your buy-sell agreement and look at two things: the date and the number. If either is more than three years old, that is the first thing to fix. Then look at your plan through Growth, Liquidity and Control: what you want the company to become, what your family can reach if you cannot, and who decides.

If you would like to walk through it together, call me.

article.title: Louisiana rewrote its tax code. Here is what it means for owners in 2026.
article.body:
Louisiana's 2024 special session changed more of the state tax code than any session in a generation, and 2026 is the first year the whole package is in force. If you own a company here, three changes are worth an hour with your CPA.

**Flat rates, and the entity question reopens**

Personal income tax is now a flat 3%, and the standard deduction rose to $12,500. Corporate income tax is a flat 5.5%. When the rates were graduated, the comparison between running your company as a pass-through and as a C corporation was already complicated. With flat rates on both sides, it is worth running again with real numbers, alongside the federal rules that changed in 2025. The answer may well stay the same. The point is to know.

**The tax on keeping capital is gone**

The corporate franchise tax is repealed for tax periods beginning on or after January 1, 2026. The return filed in 2025 was the last. That tax was measured on capital, which meant it grew as you kept earnings in the company. For an owner trying to build working capital for bonding, or a reserve for a slow year, keeping money in the business no longer carries that state cost.

**Sales tax went up, and it belongs in your bids**

To pay for the income tax cuts, the Legislature raised the state sales tax, with the increase scheduled to run through 2029. If you buy materials for jobs, that cost sits in every bid you price. Make sure your estimating reflects it, and that contracts priced before the change are not quietly eating it.

**What has not changed**

None of this changes the federal side, which is where most of an owner's tax bill still sits. And none of it is a reason to restructure in a hurry. It is a reason to check that the structure you chose years ago is still the right one at today's rates.

**Your next move**

Ask your CPA to rerun the entity comparison for your company at the 2026 Louisiana and federal rates, and to show you what the franchise tax repeal is worth to you this year. Then decide what to do with that room using Growth, Liquidity and Control: reinvest it, keep it as a reserve, or take it out.

If you would like that conversation to include your personal balance sheet as well as the company's, send me a note.
